text: A firewall rule, no matter how tight, still has something to filter — a public IP sitting out there waiting to be reached. Private Endpoints and PrivateLink take a different approach entirely: they remove the public exposure itself, so there's nothing left on the public internet for an attacker to even probe.

An Azure Private Endpoint creates a network interface with a private IP, inside your own VNet subnet, mapped to one specific instance of a resource — a particular storage account, not storage accounts in general. The piece that makes this invisible to your applications is a Private DNS Zone linked to the VNet: it overrides the resource's public hostname to resolve to that private IP instead, so no connection string ever has to change. Connections can require manual approval from the resource owner, or auto-approve.

AWS PrivateLink looks similar from the consumer side — an Interface VPC Endpoint creates an ENI with a private IP in your subnet, reaching either an AWS service or a custom Endpoint Service. The provider side is different: you front your own service with a Network Load Balancer and publish it as an Endpoint Service, and PrivateLink routes the consumer's traffic there with no peering, no route table changes, and no public IP involved on either side. An endpoint policy can further restrict what that connection is allowed to do.

S3 and DynamoDB support a second, genuinely different AWS mechanism: the Gateway Endpoint. It isn't an ENI at all — it's a route table entry that sends traffic for that service's IP prefix list through the endpoint instead of a NAT or internet gateway. Gateway Endpoints are free, regional, and route-based rather than DNS-based, and there's no Azure feature built the same way.

This is also why Private Endpoints replaced the older Azure Service Endpoint model rather than just extending it. A Service Endpoint only restricted which VNet or subnet could reach a resource's public IP over the Microsoft backbone — the public IP was still there, still in the path. A Private Endpoint removes it entirely, which is a difference in kind, not just in strictness.

Removing public exposure protects individual resources. The next lesson zooms out to the whole network: how hub-spoke design in Azure and VPC segmentation in AWS keep a single compromised resource from turning into a takeover of everything around it.
